Pinehurst, North Carolina
Garran Hill
Some houses hold history. This one shaped it.
— I — Provenance
The Gate · 1916
Built in 1916.
Named by Walter Hines Page.
The iron, the brick columns, the long drive curving beyond them — these are the proportions Leonard Tufts' craftsmen passed through in 1915. The gate has been open since 1916.
Walter Hines Page · 1855–1918
He named it Garran Hill.
He never spent a night here.

Page bought the land in February 1913 and sailed for London weeks later as Ambassador to the Court of St. James's. He directed the build from three thousand miles away. His son Ralph supervised on the ground. Leonard Tufts sent the craftsmen — the same men who built Pinehurst.

"Build the farm, therefore; and let me hear at every stage of that happy game."

He returned to America in December 1918. His son carried him off the train at Aberdeen station. He died at Currituck Cottage in Pinehurst on December 21, 1918 — ten days after he arrived.

“Well, Frank, I did get here after all, didn’t I?”
Walter Hines Page · Aberdeen Station · December 11, 1918
Neo-Georgian · 1915–1916

The proportions were not accidental.

Neo-Georgian. Six thousand and seventy-two square feet. Four bedrooms, four full baths, two powder rooms. Four and fifteen one-hundredths acres.

Foreman J.R. McQueen supervised the build under Leonard Tufts' craftsmen — the same men constructing Pinehurst in those years. The timber, the brick, the hardware: all specified from London by Walter Hines Page in correspondence with his son Ralph.

The drawings transferred with the property. Fifteen pages — elevations, floor plans, foundation, framing, portico, kitchen, primary suite, library built-ins, trim profiles. Every decision documented. Every decision still visible.

Seven fireplaces. Original leaded glass throughout. The herringbone brick at the portico threshold took three months to match when the restoration came. That is what the standard was.

— II — The House
Garran Hill · 1916
The door has been open since 1916.
The portico brick is original. The herringbone pattern was laid before a single interior wall was framed.
— III — The Restoration
The Restoration · 1999–2001

What was original stayed original.

The restoration did not make Garran Hill new. It made it whole again.

Original elements remain where they matter most: carved fireplace mantels, oak flooring throughout, leaded-glass sidelights, the arched fanlight at the entry, solid-wood interior doors, brass key plates. New systems were woven behind old grace.

Not renovated into anonymity. Restored back into itself.

Matching the old brick on the portico alone took three months. That is the standard to which every decision was held.

Fifteen pages of drawings -- elevations, floor plans, foundation, framing, portico, kitchen, primary suite, library built-ins, trim profiles. Every decision documented. The drawings transfer with the property.

The house keeps secrets

Garran Hill rewards
the close observer.

The curved banister. The original hardware. The way the light moves through the leaded glass at different hours.

This house was built by craftsmen who cared about things no one would ever notice — and then noticed them anyway. The secrets are still here. They reveal themselves slowly.

The house still knows how to keep a secret.

The Entry Hall
The house announces itself
the moment you cross the threshold.
Original leaded glass sidelights. Arched fanlight above the door. Original oak floors. Mahogany staircase volute — same since 1916.
The hall axis carries straight through to the library at the back — visible the moment the door opens.
The brass key plates on every door still have their original keys.
— IV — The Rooms
The Salon
They made it bigger
so they could dance.
Coffered ceiling. Georgian panel molding in a grid. Oak floors lifted, repaired, relaid exactly as they were.
Two full seating areas. Room enough to dance.
The Drawing Room
Fire going,
no one home yet.
Original Georgian carved mantel. Delft tile surround — blue and white, original to the room. Lion andirons. One of seven fireplaces — the only one with its original tile intact.
The room is ready before you are. It has always been ready.
The Dining Room
Formal by proportion.
Intimate by firelight.
Bay window on the north wall — curved, floor to ceiling, nine-pane divided lights, looking directly onto the grounds. Brass and porcelain chandelier.
Flanking the fireplace: arched shell alcoves, scalloped tops, built-in cabinet below — drawn on the restoration plans before a single piece of trim was cut.
Shell cabinets were already there. Still there now.
The Kitchen
The shell cabinets are original.
The kitchen is not. That is the point.
Built new in 2000. Reclaimed heart-pine floors — the only room in the house with heart-pine, chosen intentionally. Every surface was selected to honor what it replaced without pretending to be 1916.
The kitchen is not original to 1916. It is original to the restoration.
The Library
The room where every decision flowed through.
Dead center. Built-in on three walls.
Floor-to-ceiling shelving on three walls. Rolling ladder. French doors to the rear garden. This room sits at the axis of the first floor — every other room defers to it.
Walter Hines Page wrote the letters from London that built this house. This is where they were meant to be answered.
The Powder Room
Fuchsia chinoiserie.
A room that does not apologize.
The fuchsia wallpaper is the whole point. Chinoiserie pattern, floor to ceiling. Tennessee marble beneath it. This is the most opinionated room in the house — designed to stop you, make you look, make you feel something. The brass key plate on the door still holds its original key.
It works. It has always worked.
The Primary Suite
The whole floor belongs to it.
East wing. Second floor. Four rooms within a room.
Sitting room. Dressing room. Primary bath finished in Tennessee marble. The suite occupies the entire east wing of the second floor. Two exposures — east light at dawn, south light through the afternoon.
The scale is quiet. The scale is absolute.
— V — The Land
4.15 Acres · Pinehurst, North Carolina
In 1916, those were saplings.
Now they are a forest.
The Tufts craftsmen planted the pines. Betty Dumaine planted the rose garden, the camellias, the magnolias, the dogwoods.
The gardens have been cultivated continuously since 1959.
— VI — Stewardship
4.15 Acres · Pinehurst
In 1916, those were saplings.
Now they are a forest.
Leonard Tufts provided the craftsmen -- the same men building Pinehurst. The saltwater pool sits southwest of the house: 20 by 40 feet. The holly trees at the front corners were here when Betty Dumaine renamed it Hollycrest.
The Second Steward · 1959–1984
Betty Dumaine
1959 – 1984.

She bought the house for the horses and hounds she kept. She renamed it Hollycrest -- for the large native holly trees at the front of the home -- and made it her life.

In 1919, at nineteen, she had gone to the Edith Johnson School in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Her roommate was a young Thai woman named Khun Sangwan Chukramol. They bonded immediately. Sangwan later married Prince Mahidol of Songkla and became Srinagarindra -- the Princess Mother of Thailand, mother of two kings.

Betty ran her charities from this house. She raised funds to build schools in Northern Thailand. She founded a riding club in Pinehurst. She held birthday parties for her horses, to which the children of the village were invited. She fought to preserve the trees on Midland Road.

She planted the sycamores. She planted the Grandiflora magnolias. She installed the camellia garden beside the front entry circle. The grounds you are looking at are, in large part, hers.

Betty Dumaine -- Thanpuying, decorated friend of the Princess Mother of Thailand -- held birthday parties for her horses, to which the children of Pinehurst were invited. She fought to save the trees in the median of Midland Road. When she died in 1984, she left the house, and her remaining U.S. charity funds, to her foundation. The Princess Mother's Charities Fund of Thailand still operates today.

Garran Hill has that effect on people.

Blue Fox — My Irish Hunter — 1946 to 1969.
Betty Dumaine put the first flowers here.
Someone still does.

— VII — The Record
The Second Steward · 1959–1984

She renamed it. 1959 – 1984.

Betty Dumaine arrived in 1959. She bought the house for the horses and hounds she kept. She renamed it Hollycrest — for the large native holly trees at the front corners of the house.

At the Edith Johnson School in Cambridge she had roomed with Khun Sangwan Chukramol, who would become the Princess Mother of Thailand — mother of King Bhumibol Adulyadej. Betty Dumaine was appointed Thanpuying — the highest honor Thailand could bestow upon a woman not born Thai.

Blue Fox was her Irish Hunter. He lived from 1946 to 1969. He is buried at the back of the property under a slate cover with a brass marker.

She died in 1984. She left funds to the Thai-PM Cultural Foundation. Someone still puts flowers there.
